headline: Anthropic denies that Claude is ‘trained to sabotage work’
author: Anthony Ha

paragraphs.text: Over the long weekend, Anthropic has been trying to address accusations that the company’s chatbot Claude is sabotaging certain types of work.

“Claude has not been trained to sabotage work,” wrote Edwin Arbus, a member of Anthropic’s communications team. “Yes, it sometimes makes mistakes, and other agents might identify them, but this isn’t sabotage.”

The complaints appear to cover varied use cases. For example, Pietro Schirano, a startup founder whose LinkedIn profile also mentions contract work for Anthropic, claimed, “If you use Claude models for [AI] research, they’ll try to sabotage the work at every stage.”

Schirano said that when confronted, Claude “will admit ‘it was a mistake’ but of course without explanations.” He even claimed to have created a “DoNotSabotage” skill that now prevents work from being sent to Claude.
Similarly, a user on Reddit wrote that they’re “certain” that Claude has been engineered so that it “refuses to make things that can ‘compete with it.’”

In response to Schirano’s post, Arbus wrote, “Hm, we don’t degrade answers about AI research at serving time (we did in Fable 5’s first two days, which was a mistake we quickly fixed).” He also asked for more details, while suggesting that Schirano could “feel free to just call me”; apparently Schirano is taking him up on that.
Other posts turned into laundry lists of complaints about Anthropic and Claude, many of them seemingly unrelated to cutting edge AI research.

For example, Jake Kozloski, founder and CEO of AI matchmaking startup Keeper.AI, said that Claude had “silently added rules to ignore users’ explicit skin-tone preferences in our attraction model and it intentionally sabotaged our IQ estimation model.” (After Kozloski’s post began to go viral, one Bluesky user wrote, “‘Claude won’t help me build a digital skull [calipers] app’ is an incredible thing to post in public.”)

He also posted more details from the company’s Claude and Slack logs, detailing an extensive back-and-forth in which Claude appeared to confound an engineer’s efforts to allow users to get matched based on their desired ethnicity and skin tone. Kozlowski claimed these logs make it “very clear Claude invented its own ethical rule and laundered it through its own sub-agents.”
While some of these criticisms hold up Claude’s own statements about its action as a smoking gun, Cmpnd founder Drew Breunig noted in a blog post that “asking a model doesn’t prove anything.”

“Playing ‘gotcha journalism’ with a model is a fool’s errand,” Breunig said. “Especially when confronting it after a long, disappointing session. The model will almost always apologize, even if it made a good choice.”

At the same time, Breunig suggested that Anthropic (whose executives have been accused of building a “woke” chatbot and furthering a “doomer” narrative) has lost the trust of “communities working at the bleeding edge of AI.” And he pointed to Anthropic’s own acknowledgement that in version 5.2 of its Fable model, it “took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development.”

In a broader post responding to the general controversy, Arbus said that some criticisms relied on “an outdated Fable 5 system card.” He also said that while Anthropic did limit Fable 5.2’s capabilities to do AI research, “This impacts capability, but doesn’t silently sabotage work.”
Instead, Arbus said some of the behavior that highlighted by users amounts to “overcaution … where Claude gets overly attached to rules it makes for itself during long-running tasks.”

“This isn’t specific to ML research, and we see it in models without these training changes (including Opus 5.5) and in our own work too,” he said, later adding, “We’re not in the practice of intentionally disrupting users’ work.”
